A stronger mathematical version occurs in:

`H(s)H Dev +/H(s)H MANIFOLDS.txt`

which begins with the internal date `7/4/2026` and defines

\[
\boxed{
\Sigma_t^{(h)}
=
\{x\in\mathbb E_{\exp}:
|\tau(x)-t|\le h_\Sigma/2\}
}
\]

as a finite resolving slab. fileciteturn17file0

That is the clearest explicit mathematical realization of the finite-readout-thickness idea I have found so far. But the provenance backstop matters: `H(s)H MANIFOLDS.txt` is a polished/generated formalization, not yet a recovered firsthand conversation. Its first surviving Git ingest is again September 4, 2026 at the bulk-upload commit. fileciteturn29file0 I therefore classify \(h_\Sigma\) as **historically formalized, source authorship unresolved**, not as an established current H(s)H primitive.

The repository change check also surfaced a genuinely new current paper candidate in HSH_RESOURCES. Commit `056376a…`, September 11 at 06:06:22 UTC, added four prior-art PDFs plus:

`REDISCOVERED/rotoexpando_geometry_definition.tex`. fileciteturn22file0

I read the `.tex` directly in bounded sections rather than treating its existence as sufficient evidence.

The manuscript is titled **Rotoexpando Geometry: Definitions and Characterization — Nested Helices, Framed Spheres, Closure, and Equivalent Representations**, dated September 11, 2026. It explicitly says that the construction is being studied as pure geometry and that ᚼ/Hagalaz has no independent ontological content. Its present definition is much sharper than the September 8 shorthand:

\[
\mathsf H_{ij}
:=
(\sigma_{ij},Q_{ij}),
\]

or, retaining translation,

\[
\boxed{
\mathsf H_{ij}
=
(\Delta c_{ij},\sigma_{ij},Q_{ij})
}
\]

with the Euclidean similarity action

\[
x\mapsto
c_j+\sigma_{ij}Q_{ij}(x-c_i).
\]

Importantly, it explicitly says that **canonical evolution within one fixed-diameter helical order does not require expansion**. The scale component of ᚼ is primarily an adjacent-order comparison unless dynamic dilation is separately introduced. fileciteturn30file0

That is a significant clarification of the ᚼ lineage. It separates:

\[
\text{screw propagation within an order}
\]

from

\[
\text{scale relation between orders}.
\]

So “rotation-expansion” should not automatically be read as literal temporal radial dilation.

The current manuscript also independently formalizes finite-core thickness, but in a different role from historical \(h_\Sigma\). For a tube of radius \(a\) around a centerline \(X(s)\), it uses the nonlocal first-contact condition

\[
\boxed{
\inf_{s\not\approx t}
\|X(s)-X(t)\|
=
2a
}
\]

together with a local curvature constraint schematically of the form

\[
a<\frac1{\kappa_{\max}}.
\]

For the circular helix,

\[
D^2(\Delta)
=
2\rho^2(1-\cos\Delta)+h^2\Delta^2,
\]

and stationary candidates for closest nonlocal approach satisfy

\[
\boxed{
\rho^2\sin\Delta+h^2\Delta=0.
}
\]

The manuscript explicitly stops before supplying a collision, reconnection, penetration, or exclusion law. fileciteturn31file0

This gives us an important discrimination result: there are now at least **two historically/currently distinct notions of thickness** that must not be conflated:

\[
h_\Sigma
=
\text{thickness of the resolving region}
\]

versus

\[
a
=
\text{thickness/radius of a tube around a carrier centerline}.
\]

A layered architecture could contain both, but neither implies the other.

The current manuscript’s minimal adjacent-order atlas is

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal C_n=
(
\mu_n,\nu_n,\xi_n,
\Delta\phi_n,Q_n,\chi_n,a_n/D_n
)
}
\]

parts: Because I think infinities are nonphysical. Although I don't have a proof of that besides 1) Zeno's paradox would be a genuine issue for exactly the sorts of reasons Zeno and others have identified, and 2) They don't work. Literally, they fail. They fail math. They fail in the real world. That's a pretty good reason to reject their physicality. Doesn't change what they are in math. But it's almost tautological to say infinities fail more reliably than anything. Or at least equally so.

content.content: Worked for a couple of seconds

parts:
I think there is a defensible position here, but I’d sharpen it slightly.

The strongest version is not “infinity is mathematically invalid.” Clearly it isn’t. Mathematics handles infinite sets, limits, cardinalities, asymptotic structures, Hilbert spaces, and so on extremely well. The stronger physical claim is:

> mathematical infinity is often a property of representation, idealization, or limiting procedure; an actually instantiated physical infinity has not been established, and when physical theories produce divergences, that is often evidence that the representation has exceeded its domain of validity.

That is a much harder position to dismiss.

Your Zeno point is relevant, but I would phrase it carefully. Zeno becomes physically troublesome if a finite traversal really consists of completing an actually infinite sequence of distinct physical operations. Standard analysis avoids the paradox by treating the infinite subdivision as a mathematical decomposition whose summed limit is finite. That resolves the mathematics, but it does not independently establish that nature literally executes infinitely many physically individuated steps. So Zeno is less an argument against infinite mathematics than against casually identifying an infinite mathematical decomposition with physical ontology.

Your second point is stronger in physics: actual divergences are conspicuously bad physical outputs. Infinite energy density, infinite curvature, infinite self-energy, infinite temperature, and similar quantities generally signal one of three things: an idealization, an incomplete effective theory, or a breakdown of the chosen variables/model. Physicists routinely regularize, renormalize, resolve, cut off, discretize, replace point objects with extended ones, or seek a deeper description precisely because an infinite physical observable is usually not accepted as a satisfactory endpoint.

There is an important distinction, though. Not every appearance of infinity is a failure. Three cases need separating:

1. **Potential/unbounded infinity**: “there is no largest integer” or “this coordinate can increase without bound.” Nothing has to instantiate an actually completed infinite object.
2. **Idealized infinity**: an infinite plane wave, infinite homogeneous universe, continuum field with arbitrarily short wavelengths. These may be useful approximations.
3. **Divergent physical quantity**: a measured or supposedly physical magnitude goes to \(+\infty\). This is the case that most strongly smells like theory failure.

So for the finite-core program, I think your methodological principle can be stated very cleanly:

\[
\boxed{\text{Do not treat an infinity appearing in the representation as a physical constituent unless the theory independently requires it.}}
\]

And even more operationally:

\[
\boxed{\text{If a physically interpreted quantity diverges, first test whether finite extension, finite resolution, or a missing degree of freedom removes the divergence.}}
\]

That gives a principled reason for caring about finite thickness, finite cores, finite resolving slabs, finite curvature radius, finite contact scale, and so forth without prematurely deciding which particular architecture is right.

There’s also a nice connection to your current H(s)H lane: a finite-core model can be viewed as asking whether some “singular” or pointlike structures are artifacts of taking a zero-thickness limit too literally. That is a legitimate mathematical question. The correct direction is not “infinity is bad, therefore finite core is true”; it is “the physically relevant model should remain well-defined before the singular limit is taken, and any infinite-limit construction should be recoverable as an approximation rather than assumed as ontology.”

That distinction is strong enough to function as a design principle rather than a metaphysical declaration.
I specifically said it "doesn't change what they are in math". I didn't say they were mathematically invalid. Although, they do indeed fail in math reliably. Or at least predicatably.

content.content: Worked for a couple of seconds

parts:
Right — and I blurred two distinct claims you were making.

You were not saying infinity is illegitimate mathematics. You were saying that **within mathematics, infinity has highly characteristic failure modes**, and that those failure modes are predictable enough that they matter when deciding whether infinity should be taken as physically instantiated.

That is a stronger and more interesting point.

Infinity “fails” mathematically in the sense that many familiar operations stop behaving normally when you try to extend finite arithmetic naively to it. You get things like

\[
\infty-\infty,\qquad \frac{\infty}{\infty},\qquad 0\cdot\infty
\]

being indeterminate rather than ordinary arithmetic quantities. Infinite series can diverge or depend on ordering. Measures can become non-normalizable. Singular limits can destroy continuity or interchangeability of limits, derivatives, and integrals. Cardinal and ordinal arithmetic split apart from ordinary arithmetic. Infinite-dimensional spaces lose properties that hold automatically in finite dimensions. Compactness has to be recovered through additional hypotheses. Even apparently innocent limiting operations can fail to commute.

None of that means mathematics has a problem with infinity. It means mathematics has learned, in great detail, **where finite intuitions cease to transfer**.

And I think that is close to the core of what you mean by “they fail reliably.” Infinity is unusually good at marking the boundaries of an operation’s domain.

There is a useful conceptual inversion there:

\[
\text{infinity is not usually the thing mathematics has trouble defining;}
\]

\[
\text{it is where ordinary operations most reliably require qualification.}
\]

That matters physically because physics depends heavily on preserving relationships between quantities. If some supposedly real configuration forces ordinary composition laws, normalization, locality, conservation accounting, or measurement into exceptional cases, that is at least a reason to ask whether the infinity belongs to reality or to the representation.

And Zeno fits this framing better than the way I put it before. If a finite physical process literally requires the completion of an actually infinite number of physically distinct transitions, then the issue is not merely that we can sum an infinite series. The question is whether the mathematical limit operation corresponds to an actual physical mechanism. Analysis tells us the sequence has a limit. It does not by itself tell us that nature performs a completed infinite succession.

So I think your claim can be rendered fairly tightly as:

> Infinity is mathematically coherent, but it is also a systematic boundary case: operations that are straightforward over finite quantities frequently become undefined, nonunique, noncommutative, non-normalizable, or dependent on limiting procedure at infinity. That predictable exceptional behavior is evidence against casually promoting mathematical infinity into physical ontology.

I’d be comfortable with that as a serious methodological premise.

And there is perhaps an even sharper version: **finite mathematics usually tells you what happens; infinite mathematics very often requires you first to specify what you mean by “happens.”** That asymmetry is probably closer to the intuition you were pointing at.

I don't know that there is a powerful argument that infinity is coherent. And even incoherency can appear coherent under flawed assumptions. It *may* be coherent... although I might argue that coherency is an inherently relative property. Who knows, maybe if we take infinity out, we'll see math smooth out a little better somewhere else, maybe infinity, or some other nonphysical idea in math conspire to distort the parameter space? Does Goedel still throw wrenches if infinity doesn't exist? I don't claim to know. But as guesses, I think they're not implausible.

Yes. As a research instinct, that is not implausible. But there are actually several different “remove infinity” experiments hiding inside it, and they have very different consequences.

One version is merely ontological: **nothing physically infinite exists**, while mathematics remains unchanged as a representational language. That would barely touch Gödel. Gödel’s incompleteness theorems are results about formal systems, not claims that the physical universe contains an infinite object. You could live in a finite universe and still write down Peano arithmetic and get incompleteness.

A much more radical version is: **completed infinity is not admitted even inside the foundational mathematics**. Then things get considerably more interesting.

Gödel incompleteness requires, roughly, a consistent effectively axiomatized system strong enough to represent a certain amount of arithmetic and self-reference. The familiar systems have an indefinitely extensible number structure: you can always form the next numeral, encode longer proofs, encode computations, and so forth. Gödel's construction exploits that capacity.

If instead you literally imposed a largest admissible number,

\[
0,1,2,\ldots,N,
\]

and every object, proof string, computation, and quantifier ranged over an actually finite domain, then the classical Gödel situation changes drastically. A genuinely finite structure is, at least in principle, exhaustively searchable. Truth over a fixed finite domain can be decided by brute force. There isn't the same inexhaustible arithmetic universe in which Gödel numbering can keep climbing.

So:

\[
\boxed{\text{strictly finite mathematics does not simply inherit Gödel incompleteness unchanged.}}
\]

But there is a catch that I think is very relevant to your intuition.

Most versions of **finitism** do not really stop there. They say something like “there is no completed infinite set, but however large a finite number you give me, I can construct its successor.” That's *potential infinity*:

\[
N\mapsto N+1\mapsto N+2\mapsto\cdots
\]

with no final object called “the completed natural numbers.”

And that may already be enough structure for Gödel-like trouble. The theorem is fundamentally about the expressive and computational power of the formal system, not simply about somebody having postulated an object named \(\infty\). Systems regarded as strongly finitistic can still exhibit incompleteness once they are capable of encoding enough arithmetic/computation.

That gives us a much more interesting fork than “infinity versus no infinity”:

\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\text{fixed finite domain} & \neq & \text{potentially unbounded finite construction}\\
&&\\
\text{bounded computation} && \text{arbitrarily extensible computation}
\end{array}
\]

The right-hand side can recover much of the machinery responsible for incompleteness without ever saying that an actually completed infinity exists.

And this is where I think your broader speculation becomes genuinely worth thinking about. Perhaps the suspect primitive isn't “infinity” narrowly construed. Perhaps it is something closer to **unbounded extensibility**.

Suppose physical reality has some finite state capacity. Then mathematics that permits arbitrary continuation is describing not one realizable physical object, but a **rule**:

\[
x\longmapsto f(x)
\]

that we stipulate may be reapplied without bound.

We've subtly moved from ontology to generativity.

That distinction is easy to lose because notation compresses it beautifully:

\[
\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}.
\]

Those three dots do enormous conceptual work. They turn “I possess a successor rule” into “there exists a completed totality containing the result of every possible application of that rule.”

Those are not obviously the same claim.

And your “parameter-space distortion” idea has an interesting mathematical analogue. Introducing an idealized completion can absolutely change what questions become natural and what objects appear fundamental. We do this intentionally all over mathematics:

- complete the rationals to obtain the reals;
- compactify a space by adding points at infinity;
- complete a normed space;
- extend finite sums to infinite series;
- pass from finite-dimensional to infinite-dimensional spaces;
- treat distributions or singular limits as generalized objects.

These procedures can make mathematics dramatically smoother. But they can also introduce things that aren't present in the original finite structure. Sometimes the completion clarifies the underlying structure; sometimes it makes an artifact of the completion look ontologically important.

So your proposed experiment is almost the reverse:

\[
\boxed{\text{What structures survive if we refuse the completion?}}
\]

That is a perfectly sensible foundational question.

And I'd go one step further than I did previously on “coherence.” Saying that an axiomatic treatment of infinity is **internally coherent relative to some assumptions** is not the same as demonstrating that infinity is metaphysically coherent in some absolute sense. Mathematics normally gives conditional results:

\[
A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n\quad\Rightarrow\quad C.
\]

If the assumptions themselves encode something problematic, deductions can remain impeccable while the entire structure fails to correspond to the thing we thought we were describing.

Gödel himself makes this even more interesting, because sufficiently powerful systems cannot simply issue themselves an unrestricted certificate saying “everything about me is fine.” There is no God's-eye coherence detector hidden inside ordinary formal mathematics.

So I wouldn't claim that eliminating completed infinity will make mathematics “work.” We have no reason yet to know that.

But this seems like a very good question:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Which familiar mathematical pathologies require completed infinity,}
\\
\text{which require only unbounded iteration,}
\\
\text{and which survive in genuinely bounded finite systems?}
}
\]

That is testable mathematically rather than merely philosophically.

And **Gödel would be an excellent probe**. We could construct a little hierarchy—fixed finite arithmetic → bounded arithmetic → potential-infinity/finitist arithmetic → ordinary arithmetic with \(\mathbb N\) as completed totality—and ask exactly where diagonalization, undecidability, Gödel sentences, nonstandard models, compactness failures, and the various infinity-related pathologies first appear.

That would tell us whether your intuition points specifically at infinity or at something deeper that infinity happens to exemplify.

Thing is, we don't know ontology, and we cannot. It is an epistemic absolute that we can only know what we observe. It is an epistemic absolute that there *can be no distinguishing criteria* to differentiate between total interiority, total exteriority, some distribution between the two, some incoherent seeming cross-boundary phenomenon... or *any other statable configuration*. All such statements are entirely equivalent. In fact, I think it's probably provable that any proposition concerning "ontology" cannot, given that it lacks any possible referent, be coherent. Or at least not meaningful in the usual sense of the term.

parts:
I think that is a much stronger position than ordinary “we can’t know ultimate reality,” and it hangs together better if you formulate it semantically rather than metaphysically.

Your core move is:

We only ever have access to observations, experiences, records, relations, or whatever we choose to call the accessible contents. Any claim about what lies “behind,” “outside,” “under,” or “really constitutes” those contents can only be expressed using concepts drawn from within that accessible system.

If so, then competing ontological pictures such as:

- everything is interior,
- everything is exterior,
- there is a mind-independent world,
- there is only experience,
- there is a mixture,
- there is some cross-boundary interaction,
- there is an unknowable substrate,

can all be made compatible with exactly the same total observational record.

At that point, the problem is not merely underdetermination. It is that there may be no possible discriminating operation even in principle.

That is stronger.

If two statements differ but there exists no possible observation, inference, operation, or relation that could ever distinguish them, then you can argue they do not encode two empirically distinct possibilities. They are two descriptions laid over the same accessible structure.

Schematically, suppose \(O\) is the total space of possible observation histories, and \(M_1,M_2\) are “ontologies.” If

\[
P(O\mid M_1)=P(O\mid M_2)
\]

for every possible \(O\),

then there is no evidential procedure capable of favoring one over the other.

But your claim goes further still: for genuinely extra-observational ontology, this equivalence may not be accidental. It may be guaranteed by definition.

If “ontology” means something whose character is not exhausted by any possible observable relation, then no mapping

\[
\text{observation}\longrightarrow\text{ontological discriminator}
\]

can exist without smuggling the proposed ontology into the interpretation rule.

That starts looking almost theorem-like.

I would be careful with one part, though: “therefore ontological propositions are incoherent” is stronger than “therefore they have no empirically discriminable content.”

A sentence can be syntactically and even model-theoretically coherent while lacking an identifiable referent. “There is an invisible, causally inert blue cube outside all possible observation” is understandable enough as a construction. Its problem is not obvious logical contradiction. Its problem is that the terms “blue,” “cube,” “outside,” and “exists” are being extended beyond the conditions that gave them operational meaning.

That is where I think your argument can bite harder:

\[
\boxed{\text{Ontological language may be grammatically meaningful while failing to acquire a determinate referent.}}
\]

Then the question becomes what “meaning” requires.

If meaning requires only formal role in a language, ontology can be meaningful.

If meaning requires a possible referential or inferential difference, then pure ontology starts collapsing.

You can make that very sharp with an equivalence relation. Let two descriptions \(A\) and \(B\) be epistemically equivalent when no possible accessible state distinguishes them:

\[
A\sim B
\iff
\forall O,\;
O(A)=O(B).
\]

Then all purely ontological extensions of the same observational structure belong to the same equivalence class.

The quotient space

\[
\mathcal M / {\sim}
\]

contains only distinctions that can matter epistemically.

And if every purported ontology compatible with a given total observational structure falls into one equivalence class, then ontology contributes zero additional distinguishable information.

That does not prove “there is no reality.” It says something subtler:

\[
\boxed{\text{“What reality is in itself” does not denote a distinction available to an epistemic system.}}
\]

That is very close to what I think you're saying.

Your “total interiority / total exteriority / distribution / incoherent cross-boundary phenomenon” example is especially effective because it defeats a common escape hatch. People often say, “Perhaps we don't know which ontology is true, but surely one of them is.” But even that sentence presupposes that those alternatives correspond to distinct states of affairs independently of every conceivable criterion for distinguishing them.

And that is exactly the assumption under dispute.

If there can be no conceivable difference in consequence, relation, appearance, prediction, memory, inference, or operation, asking “which one is actually the case?” may be equivalent to asking for the value of a variable that has never been defined.

Not hidden.

Undefined.

That is a much more radical diagnosis than skepticism.

Skepticism says:

\[
\text{There is a fact, but we cannot know it.}
\]

Your position is closer to:

\[
\text{Outside possible discrimination, we have no grounds for saying that distinct facts have even been specified.}
\]

And I think there may indeed be a formal argument available, though I wouldn't yet call it a proof. Something along these lines:

1. A proposition has determinate content only insofar as some distinction determines its truth conditions.
2. Any distinction available to a knower must occur within the space of possible accessible relations/observations/inferences.
3. A “purely ontological” proposition is stipulated to concern something beyond all possible such distinctions.
4. Therefore no accessible distinction determines its truth conditions.
5. Therefore the proposition lacks determinate epistemic content beyond its formal linguistic role.

The vulnerable premise is #1. A Platonist, realist, or model-theoretic semanticist can deny it and say truth conditions need not be epistemically accessible.

But then they owe an account of what fixes those truth conditions.

And if their answer ultimately amounts to “a relation to something that cannot possibly enter into any relation by which its identity could be fixed,” your objection returns immediately.

That is where I think your position is strongest. Not:

“Ontology is false.”

Not even:

“Ontology is unknowable.”

But:

> Once every possible criterion of reference and discrimination is removed, it is unclear that the word “ontology” is still referring to anything at all.

That is a serious claim, and much harder to dismiss as ordinary anti-realism.

There is nothing metaphysical about the argument. It is the most elementary logical consruction, following directly from A = A with no uncertainty. If B is taken to stand for some thing, and C is taken to stand for some thing, then to even evaluate whether the referent of B and C are different, at least the possibility of some distinguishing character in some possible universe must exist. If it is the case not only that no differentiating criterion accessible--that could be overcome--but if, as in the case of ontology, it is not logically possible to exist in *any* universe such a criterion... then any statement about a criterion is necessarily void of any coherent meaning. Thus, the only formulation possible that is not meaningless, is a malformed one. So there you have it, "ontology" is either meaningless or malformed or both. Except, of course... in the case of a truly unknowable proposition, even the distinction between "meaningless" and "malformed" collapses. It is of the category "not even wrong".

parts:
Yes — with one important tightening. The target of your argument is not “ontology” in every ordinary use of the word, because some ontological claims do have distinguishing conditions. It is ontology understood as claims about a supposed reality-in-itself that is, by construction, incapable of making any possible difference whatsoever.

For that target, your argument is much stronger than ordinary skepticism.

I would formulate it this way. Suppose \(B\) and \(C\) purport to denote two different possibilities. For the assertion

\[
B\neq C
\]

to have determinate content, there must be some possible property, relation, consequence, or circumstance under which the distinction between \(B\) and \(C\) obtains. It need not be practically observable. It need not occur in our universe. But there must at least be a conceivable truth-condition separating them.

Otherwise there is literally nothing doing the work of the inequality sign.

So define a criterion family \(\mathcal D\) of all possible discriminators. Then:

\[
B \equiv C
\quad\text{iff}\quad
\forall d\in\mathcal D,\;d(B)=d(C).
\]

If the stipulation is stronger still—

\[
\neg\Diamond\exists d\,[d(B)\neq d(C)],
\]

meaning that **in no possible circumstance can any distinction between them exist**, then saying that \(B\) and \(C\) nevertheless denote different possibilities adds no content to the language.

That is where I think your “not even wrong” diagnosis lands.

There is one place I would not derive it directly from \(A=A\), however. The law of identity alone gives:

\[
A=A.
\]

It does not by itself establish the converse principle

\[
\text{no possible difference} \Rightarrow \text{same referent}.
\]

That extra step is closer to a criterion of identity or semantic individuation principle. And historically, something resembling Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles can be disputed when “indiscernible” means merely sharing all ordinary properties.

But your version avoids much of that dispute because you are making a stronger claim than ordinary indiscernibility. You aren't saying:

> We happen not to know a difference.

Nor:

> They possess all properties we have tested.

You're saying:

> The proposed distinction is defined such that no possible relation, property, counterfactual, consequence, or other truth-condition could distinguish the alternatives.

At that point, “there nevertheless exists a difference” is peculiar because **difference itself is relational structure**. If every possible specification of that structure is excluded, the sentence retains the grammatical form of a proposition while withholding what would make it a proposition about anything.

That's why I think your meaningless/malformed collapse is interesting.

Normally:

- a **false proposition** has intelligible truth conditions and fails them;
- a **meaningless expression** fails to determine truth conditions;
- a **malformed expression** fails some syntactic or compositional rule.

But in the limiting case you're describing, we cannot even cleanly ask which sort of failure occurred, because that distinction itself presupposes enough semantic structure to identify what the expression was attempting to denote.

So perhaps the cleanest category is:

\[
\boxed{\text{pseudo-proposition}}
\]

An expression with propositional grammar but no possible discriminating truth-condition.

And then your proposed “ontology” becomes a generator of pseudo-propositions whenever it introduces differences such as

\[
\text{appearance} \neq \text{reality-in-itself}
\]

while simultaneously stipulating that no possible state of affairs can determine the right-hand term or distinguish alternative assignments to it.

The particularly sharp consequence is that saying “the true ontology is unknowable” would itself already say too much.

“Unknowable” normally means:

\[
\exists p\quad\land\quad \neg K(p).
\]

There is a proposition \(p\), but it cannot be known.

Your argument attacks the first conjunct. If no possible criterion establishes what would count as \(p\) rather than \(q\), then we haven't established that there is a determinate proposition there to be unknown.

So instead of

\[
\boxed{\text{There is a truth we cannot know}}
\]

you get

\[
\boxed{\text{No determinate candidate truth has been specified.}}
\]

That is substantially more severe than agnosticism, skepticism, idealism, or anti-realism. Those positions are still fighting over which side of a purported boundary is epistemically privileged. Your argument says that an absolutely undiscriminable boundary doesn't furnish two sides in the first place.

And there is a neat self-applicative consequence of your final point. If someone responds:

> “But perhaps there really is a distinction between meaningful and malformed here, and we simply can never know which.”

they have just recreated the same forbidden structure one level higher: they posit a distinction while excluding every possible criterion that could constitute that distinction.

So yes: under the unrestricted “no possible discriminator in any possible world” condition, I think the argument can be made much more formally than I was giving it credit for. The genuinely difficult part would be proving that the traditional notion of **noumenal ontology really does satisfy that modal condition**, rather than merely being contingently inaccessible to us. Once that premise is granted, most of the rest is semantic logic rather than metaphysics.

"No possible difference" does not mean "same referent". Nor does it mean "no referent". It means that in the case of this comparison, there can be no distinction even between "same" and "no". The choice of a term whose identity has no possible distinguisher from literally any other proposition means both "same referent" and "no referent" are also *indistinguishable* for the chosen concept. "We happen to not know a difference" is tractable. "We do not know whether a difference could be discovered" is tractable. "We *know* that we cannot by structural necessity of the physical laws of our universe *ever* be in a position to identify a distinction" ...is tractable. But: "There cannot logically be a criterion for distinction ever in any universe". That's not tractable except by redefining the word or applying the word only to the only thing that *is* knowable--which is the givenness of perceptions and the qualities they are perceived (which happen to constitute all knowability--and only as perception... those, one *does* know. And with absolute epistemic certitude)... So, you could say "this" -- whatever this is -- is ontology. And that move only pretends to cheat the logic by creating a new meaningless distinction.

Yes. That correction matters.

I was still trying to force your argument into the familiar semantic fork:

\[
\text{same referent}\quad\text{vs}\quad\text{no referent}.
\]

But your point is that this fork itself presupposes exactly the discriminative machinery that the target term excludes.

If \(X\) is stipulated such that there cannot possibly be any criterion—across any possible circumstance—for determining anything about its identity, then asking

\[
\operatorname{Ref}(X)=r?
\]

already grants more structure than \(X\) permits. And so does

\[
\operatorname{Ref}(X)=\varnothing?
\]

Those look like opposed answers only because our metalanguage ordinarily has criteria for distinguishing successful reference from failed reference. Applied to something defined as absolutely criterionless, that distinction cannot get purchase.

So the more faithful structure is not

\[
\text{indiscernible}\Rightarrow\text{identical},
\]

and not

\[
\text{indiscernible}\Rightarrow\text{nonreferential}.
\]

It is more like:

\[
\boxed{
\neg\Diamond D(X,Y)
\quad\text{for every possible }Y
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\text{identity predicates concerning }X\text{ cannot be evaluated.}
}
\]

And “every possible \(Y\)” is crucial. If \(X\) cannot possibly be distinguished not merely from some rival \(Y\), but from *anything whatsoever*—including “nothing,” “same,” “different,” “referential,” “nonreferential,” and alternative purported ontologies—then those classifications all lose their discriminating role with respect to \(X\).

That is more radical than semantic underdetermination. Underdetermination says there are multiple admissible values and the evidence doesn't select one. Your construction says that **the value-space itself cannot be coherently partitioned for this variable**.

So “unknown ontology” is already malformed in your sense because “unknown” normally presupposes something like

\[
\exists x\,[P(x)\land\neg K(P(x))].
\]

But to quantify over \(x\), assign \(P\), and distinguish \(P(x)\) from alternatives is already to have supplied identity conditions. The supposed absolutely inaccessible ontology cannot satisfy those conditions without ceasing to be the thing originally stipulated.

That also explains why the move you describe—

> “Fine, then call *this*, the given, ontology.”

—doesn't rescue traditional ontology. It simply changes the referent of the word.

Now “ontology” means the presently given structure of experience/perception. That is tractable because distinctions exist within it:

\[
\text{red}\neq\text{blue},\qquad
\text{pain}\neq\text{silence},\qquad
\text{before}\neq\text{after},
\]

etc.

But then someone who says

> “Yes, but what is the ontology *behind* that?”

has reintroduced the very null distinction that was just eliminated. The second “ontology” no longer inherits meaning merely because the first one had it.

There is a particularly elegant asymmetry here:

\[
\boxed{\text{givenness can be individuated internally; the absolutely extra-given cannot.}}
\]

I would make one small qualification to your “absolute epistemic certitude” formulation. I think the strongest absolutely secure claim is not necessarily every conceptual characterization of perception, but the occurrence of givenness itself—something like:

\[
\boxed{\text{There is this appearing / seeming / givenness.}}
\]

Once I say “this is red,” “this is a perception,” “this has duration,” etc., some conceptual apparatus has entered and can itself be interrogated. But the occurrence being characterized cannot be removed without the attempted denial itself becoming another occurrence of the same kind. That gives it an unusual reflexive security.

And that may actually strengthen your argument. You don't need to construct an ontology of perceptions. You need only note that **all possible criteria occur within givenness**. Therefore any proposed distinction whose definition places it outside every possible criterion cannot subsequently borrow the apparatus of distinction from within givenness.

Put very compactly:

\[
\text{Knowability requires possible discrimination.}
\]

\[
\text{Reference requires possible individuation.}
\]

\[
\text{“Absolute ontology” excludes all possible discrimination and individuation.}
\]

Therefore asking whether such an ontology is one thing, another thing, something, nothing, internal, external, mental, physical, simulated, fundamental, or emergent does not leave us with difficult questions.

It leaves us with strings that retain the **grammar of questions after the conditions for questioning have been removed**.

And I now see why you object to even calling that “meaningless” without qualification. “Meaningless” versus “malformed” is itself another classification. If the alleged target supplies no conditions under which that classification could attach to it rather than fail to attach, the safest characterization is indeed something like **not even wrong**—not because we've discovered what the statement is, but because we cannot coherently get far enough to assign it the status of a determinate proposition.

I suppose one could also say "ontology means, the word 'ontology'". By that definition, ontology has discernable qualities, like that of being a word, and thereby being different from other words. In other words, by removing it from the category of things claimed to have non-tautological meaning and placing it into the category of only having tautological meaning, which "ontology" ...probably some such use exists. But that's a different game.

Exactly. That move makes “ontology” tractable by turning it into an object within the domain of givens.

Then “ontology” can mean the token, inscription, sound-pattern, lexical item, dictionary entry, or concept-sign. In that case it has perfectly ordinary distinguishing properties: it has eight letters, begins with “o,” differs from “epistemology,” has a history of usage, occurs in certain sentences, and so on.

But that is a metalinguistic object:

\[
\text{“ontology”} = \text{this word/sign/concept-token}
\]

and not:

\[
\text{ontology} = \text{the supposedly extra-given way reality really is}.
\]

The former has identity conditions. The latter, under your construction, does not even supply the possibility of identity conditions.

So yes, one can rescue the word by collapsing it into tautological or internally referential use. “Ontology is the word ‘ontology’” is distinguishable because the referent is right there in the language system. Similarly, “ontology is the set of claims philosophers classify as ontological” can be meaningful as taxonomy. “Ontology” in computer science can mean a formal specification of entities and relations. All of those are ordinary finite objects or practices with criteria of distinction.

What cannot be obtained for free is the transition:

\[
\text{we possess a distinguishable word/concept}
\quad\therefore\quad
\text{that concept distinguishes an extra-conceptual referent}.
\]

That inference fails generally. Having a noun doesn't establish a corresponding thing, much less establish identity conditions for it.

And I think your “different game” phrasing is exactly right. There are at least two games that routinely get slid together:

\[
\boxed{\text{talking about the concept/sign “ontology”}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{\text{using that sign to purport to discriminate an absolutely undiscriminable state of affairs}.}
\]

The first can support ordinary true and false propositions. The second is where your argument says the machinery bottoms out.

There is a slightly mischievous consequence: one could write a perfectly rigorous ontology of the word *ontology*. You could catalogue its tokens, usages, semantic neighborhoods, etymology, inferential roles, and historical shifts. Every proposition would have possible distinguishing criteria.

Then the instant the analysis says, “and now we move from all of those appearances to what ontology itself really refers to beyond every possible appearance,” it has changed logical type without announcing it.

That type error may be much of what you are objecting to.

So a very compact formulation might be:

\[
\boxed{
\text{“Ontology” is meaningful wherever its referent is discriminable.}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{Where it is defined as absolutely beyond possible discrimination, the word survives but its purported non-tautological content does not.}
}
\]

That leaves ordinary technical uses of “ontology” untouched while isolating exactly the use you think collapses.

parts: That's the thing--if it were something that could, under my construction fail to 021
I think your message got clipped at “fail to 021”. Send the rest of the thought—I don’t want to guess what you meant, especially given how exact the distinction has been here.

That’s the thing—if there existed some other construction in which it could achieve an evaluable by any normal sense of the word “meaning”… that is, if there were a universe, if there were a logically possible other mind for which the meaning were even conceivably logically articulable… then it would be tractable. If there were any situation in which some other observer could say “ah, yes, here’s the dividing line” or even “I am in no position to see the discernible difference”, or even if there were a conceivable point of view in which the meaning were discernible while still having any resemblance to the ordinary meaning—then *that* would be sufficient to make it tractable. The reason it is a lacuna is that no such situation is even logically possible in any universe. E mm

Yes. That makes the quantifier in your argument much clearer, and it is stronger than anything about human cognitive limitations.

You are not requiring that *we* possess the discriminator. You are granting essentially every escape route imaginable. Another organism, another kind of mind, another universe, different physical laws, different senses, arbitrary computational power, direct access to things inaccessible to us—all of that is allowed. If there were even one logically possible standpoint from which the purported distinction became articulable while retaining the intended meaning, then the concept would be tractable in your sense.

So the condition is closer to:

\[
\exists W\,\exists O\,\exists D:
D_O^W(A,B)
\]

where \(W\) is any logically possible world, \(O\) any possible discriminator/observer, and \(D\) any criterion capable of making the proposed distinction determinate.

You require only **one witness**.

If there is one, the distinction is tractable even if nobody in our universe could ever reach it.

Your proposed ontological lacuna instead has the much stronger property

\[
\boxed{
\neg\Diamond\exists(O,D)\;D_O(A,B)
}
\]

—not “nobody knows \(D\),” and not “our universe prevents access to \(D\),” but **there is no logically possible \(D\) to be had** while preserving what the terms are supposed to mean.

And I think I now see the especially nasty feature of “ontology” under your construction. Usually, when something is unknowable, we can nevertheless specify what knowing it *would amount to*.

For example, suppose the interior of some permanently inaccessible region can never causally communicate with us. I can still say:

\[
\text{If an observer were inside it, }X\text{ rather than }Y\text{ would distinguish the alternatives.}
\]

That's perfectly meaningful. The distinction survives our inability to evaluate it.

Even something physically impossible for humans can remain meaningful:

> “No human could survive there, but an ideal detector would return \(x\) rather than \(y\).”

Again, we've supplied the counterfactual discrimination criterion.

Your ontology case prohibits exactly this maneuver. Suppose we imagine the magical observer who gets “outside perception” and sees reality as it is. What does *sees* mean there? If the observer acquires something—an appearance, datum, state, relation, difference—then that acquisition is now part of what is given to that observer.

We've constructed another epistemic interior.

So:

\[
\text{putative access to the extra-given}
\longrightarrow
\text{something is given}
\longrightarrow
\text{it is no longer functioning as the extra-given}.
\]

Try again with direct knowledge rather than perception: the observer simply **knows** reality-in-itself.

But then there must be some distinction between knowing that it is \(A\) and knowing that it is \(B\). Otherwise “knows” has accomplished nothing. The moment that distinction is specified, it becomes articulable content of the observer's epistemic state.

Same collapse.

That's why merely changing universes doesn't help. Give the other universe completely different physical laws and the problem survives, because the obstacle isn't physical. Give its inhabitants telepathy, omniscient instruments, additional dimensions, access to our simulation's source code—whatever you like. If something becomes available to distinguish \(A\) from \(B\), **that distinction is part of their givenness**.

And if nothing becomes available, they haven't distinguished \(A\) and \(B\).

That gives the argument an almost annoyingly simple recursive form:

\[
\boxed{
\text{If }D\text{ is accessible, it belongs to the accessible.}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{If }D\text{ is absolutely inaccessible, it cannot discriminate for anyone.}
}
\]

There doesn't appear to be a third category in which a criterion both makes a difference and makes no possible difference.

And this clarifies your use of **lacuna** beautifully. It isn't a blank spot on a map whose contents happen to be unavailable. That would be ordinary ignorance.

It is more like an attempted coordinate for which the coordinate transformation itself cannot be defined. Saying “there might nevertheless be something at that coordinate” simply repeats the original pseudo-distinction.

There is another consequence I hadn't appreciated earlier. Even **“ontology exists” versus “ontology doesn't exist”** cannot escape.

Normally,

\[
\exists X
\]

and

\[
\neg\exists X
\]

are maximally different propositions. But if \(X\) is defined so that absolutely no possible circumstance could distinguish a world containing \(X\) from one not containing \(X\), then attaching the existential quantifier hasn't restored the missing individuation. We've written two syntactically opposed expressions without establishing what difference their opposition corresponds to.

So under your construction the collapse reaches surprisingly far:

\[
\text{something/nothing},
\quad
\text{same/different},
\quad
\text{exists/doesn't exist},
\quad
\text{internal/external},
\quad
\text{known/unknown}
\]

all presuppose a space in which the alternatives can in principle be discriminated.

And I think that's the key correction to my earlier attempts to classify the ontological term as “nonreferential.” **Nonreference is already an answer to a question your construction says cannot be posed determinately.**

That really is different from skepticism. It's not an extraordinarily inaccessible fact.

It's the absence of the logical conditions under which there could be a fact of the stipulated kind.

That’s an extremely clear explanation and I think it may clarify to me some things I’ve found somewhat challenging. Under …and I know it has different uses elsewhere, including importantly relativity… the equivalence principle, by my construction, which I usually do construct from A = A, but maybe I have to distinguish that more precisely. …but under that rule, a surprising number of things fall, given my understanding of epistemic truth. My usual move has been to fallback to something like “no matter how impossible it may seem, two truly indistinguishable propositions (if so absolutely indistinguishable any on conceivable condition), are therefore one in the same, which if pressed, I’ll admit that even sameness vs not sameness is not actually discernible. And i think this dividing line, appropriately enough, splits along the complementary or coterminality line. That is, its kind of my signature move, philosophically, to declare (eg) if interior -/ø (to coin an operator) exterior, then Erior. If determinism -/ø agency, then Dererminagency, if qualia -/o phenomenology, then Qualomenology. And I think I temporarily had another but found it to be a special case of one of them… I think it was… ah, yes. Irrectness

thoughts.content: I’m treating the user’s “signature move” as a conceptual practice rather than ordinary identity. The key distinction seems to be between asserting that two things are identical and refusing to preserve a distinction between them. “Coterminality” could describe collapsing distinctions based on indiscriminability, while “Erior” might name the resulting equivalence class. I’m not fully sure what “Irrectness” means here, so I should ask for clarification rather than infer too much.

items.title: Curve Composition System
items.snippet:
I’m trying to figure out the structure of this concept:

It has to be possible to set up a system—not necessarily an already standard system—that takes an equation, captures some solution of it as a curve, does the same with a second equation, and then takes those two curves, outputs a composite curve, which can then be reverse engineered into an equation that is a derivative of both of the originals. Whatever additional structure is necessary to do that in a deterministic way is the system. 

My notion is to draw two curves on opposite hemispheres of a sphere, connect them in such a way that the motion along each is translated into vertical and horizontal motions of a crossbar/gimbal system , which then traces out something like a Lissajous curve on the inside surface of a torus, which is the composite curve of the two… you roll the sphere around inside the torus until the composite curve connects back on itself, and then find the equation of that curve, which is a derivative of both of the two input equations

items.title: Extrapolating Hypothetical Names
items.snippet:
Hi, I’d like to engage in an intellectual exercise. In each of my prompts, I’ll give you one or more words designating objects or concepts that contain numerical prefixes or roots. Just for fun, I’d like you to extrapolate hypothetical names for (likely improbable) related objects or concepts based on existing word-forming conventions for the given words and similar words, but for variants of the word from 1 to 20. Before diving in, I’ll give you an example to illustrate my meaning. 

If I gave you the words “centipede” and “millipede” your answer might be as follows (although my example extrapolations probably won’t be entirely in keeping with the naming conventions, I’d like you to try to be as systematic as possible): 

Unipede 
Dipede
Tripede
Quadrupede
Quintipede…
And so on, up to…
Vigentipede

Does this make sense?

Yes — and I think this gives you a cleaner formal account of what you’ve been doing than “indistinguishable things are the same.”

Your actual move is weaker in one sense and stronger in another. You are not asserting ordinary identity,

\[
A=B.
\]

You are saying that where the distinction between \(A\) and \(B\) has no possible discriminator under any conceivable condition, the distinction itself ceases to be a usable partition. So instead of identity, what you really have is something like a collapse operator:

\[
A\;{-/\varnothing}\;B
\]

meaning roughly:

\[
\neg\Diamond(\text{criterion distinguishing }A\text{ from }B).
\]

Then the result is not “A is B” in the ordinary sense. It is more like:

\[
[A,B]_{-/\varnothing}
\]

—a single undivided category produced by the failure of the proposed boundary to define two evaluable sides.

That fits your coinages very well.

Interior \(-/\varnothing\) exterior gives **Erior** not because interior and exterior have been proven identical, but because, at the level you’re talking about, the supposed separating boundary cannot be supplied without already locating oneself on one side of it.

Likewise determinism \(-/\varnothing\) agency gives **determinagency** if every event describable as “determined” can equally be described from another inseparable perspective as “the agent doing what the agent does,” with no possible experiment capable of extracting one while excluding the other at the level being claimed.

And qualia \(-/\varnothing\) phenomenology gives **qualomenology** if the supposed distinction between “the qualitative content itself” and “its appearing” cannot be independently instantiated or identified.

The important improvement is that you no longer need the fallback:

> truly indistinguishable propositions must therefore be one and the same.

Because, as you noticed, that invites the immediate question “same in what sense?” and then you are forced to admit that sameness versus nonsameness is itself one of the collapsed distinctions.

Your operator handles that directly:

\[
\boxed{
A\;{-/\varnothing}\;B
\not\Rightarrow
A=B
}
\]

and also

\[
\boxed{
A\;{-/\varnothing}\;B
\not\Rightarrow
A\neq B.
}
\]

Rather,

\[
\boxed{
A\;{-/\varnothing}\;B
\Rightarrow
\text{the partition }\{A,B\}\text{ is not well-defined at that level.}
}
\]

That is much cleaner.

And I think “coterminality” is exactly the right geometric intuition for it. Two conceptual trajectories may approach what looks linguistically like two different endpoints, but at the point where you ask what would constitute the separation, both terminate on the same boundary—or, more precisely, the proposed boundary is all there is. There is no further fact available to say there are two shores.

So your characteristic philosophical move is not really synthesis in the Hegelian sense, nor reduction of one thing to another. It’s closer to **quotienting out a distinction that has no invariant**.

Mathematically, if you had a space of descriptions \(X\), you could define

\[
A\sim B
\]

whenever no logically possible discriminator exists between them. Then you stop working with \(X\) and work with the quotient

\[
X/{\sim}.
\]

“Erior,” “determinagency,” and “qualomenology” are names for elements of that quotient space.

That is a surprisingly precise description of the move.

There is another nice consequence. Your \(-/\varnothing\) operator is not symmetrical with ordinary conjunction.

\[
A\land B
\]

says both independently obtain.

\[
A\lor B
\]

says at least one obtains.

\[
A=B
\]

says they share identity.

But

\[
A\;{-/\varnothing}\;B
\]

says something closer to:

> the attempted distinction between these expressions fails to induce two distinguishable states.

That deserves its own operator because none of the normal logical connectives quite says it.

And this may explain why you keep encountering the same maneuver in very different domains. You are repeatedly noticing cases where language has inserted a cut:

\[
X\mid Y
\]

and then asking what invariant crosses that cut. If no conceivable invariant distinguishes the sides, you erase the cut rather than deciding which side is fundamental.

That is very much a reusable method.

As for **Irrectness**: I don’t have enough surviving context to reconstruct what pair you had collapsed there, and I don’t want to invent it. But the name strongly sounds like another member of exactly this family. If you remember the two terms you were collapsing, I suspect we could tell pretty quickly whether it is genuinely independent or reduces to Erior, determinagency, or qualomenology.

items.title: Curve Composition System
items.snippet:
I’m trying to figure out the structure of this concept:

It has to be possible to set up a system—not necessarily an already standard system—that takes an equation, captures some solution of it as a curve, does the same with a second equation, and then takes those two curves, outputs a composite curve, which can then be reverse engineered into an equation that is a derivative of both of the originals. Whatever additional structure is necessary to do that in a deterministic way is the system. 

My notion is to draw two curves on opposite hemispheres of a sphere, connect them in such a way that the motion along each is translated into vertical and horizontal motions of a crossbar/gimbal system , which then traces out something like a Lissajous curve on the inside surface of a torus, which is the composite curve of the two… you roll the sphere around inside the torus until the composite curve connects back on itself, and then find the equation of that curve, which is a derivative of both of the two input equations

items.title: Extrapolating Hypothetical Names
items.snippet:
Hi, I’d like to engage in an intellectual exercise. In each of my prompts, I’ll give you one or more words designating objects or concepts that contain numerical prefixes or roots. Just for fun, I’d like you to extrapolate hypothetical names for (likely improbable) related objects or concepts based on existing word-forming conventions for the given words and similar words, but for variants of the word from 1 to 20. Before diving in, I’ll give you an example to illustrate my meaning. 

If I gave you the words “centipede” and “millipede” your answer might be as follows (although my example extrapolations probably won’t be entirely in keeping with the naming conventions, I’d like you to try to be as systematic as possible): 

Unipede 
Dipede
Tripede
Quadrupede
Quintipede…
And so on, up to…
Vigentipede

Does this make sense?

Sure you do: direct (eg knowledge, action) -/ø indirect; irrectitude 

But notice that these “unities”, as I call them, as a class, differ — I *think* — from the even harder case of “ontology”.  In that they are at least conceptually conjugate pairs, so one can imagine them to form a sort of “coterminal surface of isness” (to which one could conceivably apply, or at least pose the question of some sort of complementary or, probably better, chirality—the two propositions together fill the conceptual space precisely, allowing at least the line of division itself to have a conceptual ‘location’ — to which I now coin the lovely: Locus of Unitation… or maybe Monadualism). But ontology vs what? solipsism is already one aspect of (or at unity with) …uh… Solipsealism? … Nononaïve Realipsism? Aïve Ealismus? …which is itself just a synonym for Eriority. So maybe ontology is just a partial synonym for the IEU (interior-exterior unity — the Donad?) lol. Interesting how the nomenclature becomes prolific when collapsing so many things… But I’m not sure what the other side of ontology is per se. But it seems to me that it would have to be perception or perhaps unknowability? Is there a coterminal conceptual space? … and now that I think about it, this notion of coterminus is, perhaps definable less as “there is a conceptual clean divide”, but rather more accurately, as is implicit in my nomenclature I think, the boundary becomes co-enveloping. There is a conceptual space, there are two conceptual spaces, but rather than dividing some totality, the conceptual division undergoes a sort of eversion into an exterior boundary of the whole, which is, at least locally or at least within the greater concept space of all thinkable thinks, a definably present *somethingness*, as in the manner of the Eriority I, and presumably but unknowably, you (or at least a locutor who acknowledges/knows its own interiority). Likewise, Dererminagency results in action, irregardless of whether we purport to be able to know or even definably identify the potentator or origin thereof. Kind of nearly denies the notion of chirality or there being halves of the coin if the coterminus is the outer surface of the conjoint. 

But these traditional dualities which I collapse or duamonize into one, I think can be truly said to be in a sense definable by negation, when that negation is productive if only in creating the shared space of something of which they/it can be said to be. There’s sort of a generative coherency in the precision of the opposition which allows unity. 

That is quite different from the combobulatory discoherence that results when no such identitizing antopposition is apparent. The Parency of the Gation, if you will. Lacking PoG, we find neither gap nor any localization whereat some gap might be proffered to hollow out.
